posts.title: SNAPTRAP
posts.summary: buzz buzz...you're a fly...reach in for a snack?

body.text:
Material choice was important for a game with high player traffic. The faux pink alligator leather made it easy to wipe down the installation, and to keep players' limbs intact, I added pool noodle padding on the edges and increased the height of the hinge. Our pincers were also printed with an iridescent, beetle-shell like filament.

The entire installation can be broken down into a large suitcase, and the pink pleather can be peeled back easily to debug flex sensors and their wiring.

Real venus flytraps attract flies with nectar and snap shut once two hairs are triggered in succession. The delicate balance between collaboration and competition led to fascinating group dynamics. Triggering one hair makes it so if another hair is touched, everyone loses. Players as a group had to decide if it was worth it or not to continue grabbing nectar.

The physical nature and open-ended rules of our game led to some really interesting emergent gameplay and strategies. Some players hoarded nectar on their side, some stole from others, and bolder ones fought other players for preferred pieces.

Our pincer shapes also left a lot to personal preference. Players found creative ways to use their "jaws"!
The trap's run may be nearing the end, but I've learned a lot from working on the fabrication and a bit of the hardware side. Maybe I'll find a permanent place to display it?

posts.title: Spellfish
posts.summary: cast spells and your fishing line to reel in magical beasts.

body.text:
Every good game has a beloved fishing minigame. I've loved playing *Stardew Valley* and *Animal Crossing*, but I'd always wished for the chance to show off flashy combos and strategy while reeling in my catches.

I looked toward games like *League of Legends* and *Hearthstone* for their cohesive magical visual style, while splashing a bit of *Animal Crossing*'s coziness in the form of softer, inviting shapes and friendly colors.

**Visuals combine the nautical and arcana, with the rugged, freeform shapes of sailing motifs mixed with the graceful and geometric forms of the arcane.** Accents are gold, with small pops of saturated highlights. Small details of trim, dangling jewelry or ropes give a witchy energy.

To catch such slippery creatures, players must choose *Spells* and *Enchantments* wisely. **Spells are active abilities, and Enchantments are passive buffs that change up gameplay in new and exciting ways.**

Players choose cards that fit their preferred playstyle - those who enjoy performing steady combos will prefer water type spells, while those who prefer to play with fire (high risk, high reward spells) will gravitate towards fire cards.

Every time players catch a fish, they get a Token of the Fish's Blessing - these can be spent to craft powerful tarot cards, or disenchanted into bait to catch more fish.

Players are also able to craft Tokens into tarot cards. (Mana on left, element on right)
When players catch a fish for the first time, it is added into their journal. Card backgrounds evoke tarot aesthetics and reflect the fish's rarity - common, rare, or legendary.
While this project is on the backburner, I'd like to update some of the card art and buttons sometime :)

posts.title: Stranger Things VR

body.text: I concepted and created diegetic layouts, assets, and effects based on 1980s style interfaces and IP guidelines.  Interfaces had to integrate with the rest of the world - no HUDs and fewer floating displays that would break immersion.

I had a great time working within the constraints of 1980s tech and GUI design trends (I now know an odd amount about segmented displays!). 
Diegetic UI made for a rewarding task to design clear and engaging interfaces that worked with - and not just "on top of" - the environment and surroundings.
*(UI pics coming)*

posts.title: Scan-It Planet
posts.summary: scan real objects to solve platforming puzzles.

body.text:
Scan-it Planet is an asymmetrical co-op multiplayer game where one player navigates via controller while other players move physical objects over the scanner to create bridges over platforms. 

We focused on encouraging creative problem solving. To form bridges, some players used objects from their pockets, some used limbs, and others used the provided cardboard pieces. Kids loved working in a team, and there was a place for everyone no matter their prior experience with gaming!

As an exhibitor, we needed to onboard players quickly. I made a short tutorial after noticing where players struggled. Bombs in particular were confusing, since they required players to readjust their scanned objects to avoid them.

Scanned objects and platforms are very distinct from the background, and hazards communicate danger through their color and shapes to make it understandable to players of all ages.

Coming from mostly digital work, I didn’t expect to be looking up the length of the average arm (to map out our play area) or thinking about installation setup and teardown. After a couple of enclosure iterations, we settled on a modified wire shelf: lightweight, open-air, and easy to take apart. Our local Python server handled computer vision (to separate out scanned objects) and we used Unity for the game itself.

posts.intro:
Scan physical objects to bridge gaps in the digital world. Help your tiny astronaut friend explore a new planet with your superpowered scanner!
